# Vignette: Nadia, Age 19

Nadia was sixteen when her younger brother stopped breathing at the dinner table.

He had been sick for a few weeks — a fever that kept returning, bruises that appeared without explanation, a tiredness that made him quiet in a way he never was. Her parents had taken him to the doctor twice, but no one had said the word leukemia yet. That word came later, at the hospital, after the paramedics had worked over him on the kitchen floor while Nadia stood in the doorway holding a dish towel, unable to move. She remembers the sound of her mother's voice — not words, just sound — and the particular yellow of the overhead light. For a long time afterward, yellow light felt wrong to her.

Her brother survived. He spent four months in the pediatric oncology ward, underwent chemotherapy, and is now, three years later, in remission. Most people in Nadia's life consider the story to have a happy ending. She understands why they feel that way. She does not feel that way.

What she carries is harder to name than grief, because grief is for something lost. Her brother is alive. He sits across from her at family dinners now, taller than he was, eating too fast the way he always did. And yet some part of Nadia's nervous system has never quite accepted the news that the emergency is over.

She works the early shift at a distribution warehouse on the edge of the city, sorting and moving packages from five in the morning until early afternoon. She chose the hours deliberately — not consciously at first, but she understands now that early mornings keep her busy during the stretch of time when her mind is most dangerous. Sleep has been unreliable since the night her brother collapsed. She falls asleep without difficulty most nights but wakes around three or four, heart already moving fast, sometimes from a dream and sometimes from nothing she can identify. She lies there and tries to remember that he is in his room, that his blood counts are normal, that the oncologist said the word remission. The facts are available to her. They don't always help.

At work, she is known as someone who keeps to herself but does her job without complaint. Her supervisor has noticed that she startles easily — the clang of a metal shelf, a forklift reversing with its beeping alarm — and once asked if she was okay. She said she was tired. That was true enough.

Her boyfriend, who has been with her for nearly a year, knows pieces of what happened but not the whole shape of it. She finds it difficult to explain why a healthy child in another room can still make her stop what she is doing and listen. Why she sometimes needs to physically see her brother before she can settle. Why she pulled away from her friends during those months at the hospital and has never quite found her way back to the ease she had before. She worries she is too much to be with, and she worries she is not enough. Both fears live in her at the same time.

There are moments — at the warehouse, lifting and stacking in the rhythm of physical work, or in the early morning quiet before anyone else is awake — when she feels almost like herself. But then something small happens: a child coughs in a grocery store, or she reads a word like *relapse*, or the light in a room is that particular shade of yellow, and she is back on the kitchen floor in her mind, dish towel in her hands, watching people try to save her little brother.

She is nineteen years old. She knows the story ended well. She is still waiting, somewhere inside herself, to believe it.
